title: What Happens When a State Tests Its Voucher Students
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Most states with private-school-choice programs don't require voucher-funded students to take any standardized tests, which makes it nearly impossible to answer basic questions about how those programs are working academically. Iowa is a rare exception, and its annual Condition of Education report lets the author dig into two years of data on its Education Savings Account (ESA) program. He finds that enrollment has grown quickly but has skewed sharply toward wealthier families as income caps phased out, with low-income participation dropping from 30% to 11% of recipients in a single year. Proficiency rates for ESA students look strong, but the more revealing growth-percentile data shows ESA students progressing at roughly the same rate as public-school peers with similar starting scores — no dramatic advantage, no collapse. The piece closes by noting that even Iowa's relatively transparent approach still fails parents, since the state doesn't publish school-level results, undercutting the market logic that's supposed to justify school choice in the first place.
points: Iowa is a rare exception among states with private-school-choice programs because it actually requires ESA (Education Savings Account) recipients to take the same state tests as public school students.
Enrollment data shows Iowa's ESA program has shifted sharply toward wealthier families as income caps phased out, with low-income participation falling from 30% to 11% of recipients in two years.

Proficiency rates look strong for ESA students, but growth-percentile data — a better measure of program effect — shows ESA students progressing at roughly the same rate as public-school peers with similar starting scores.

Even with more data than most states, Iowa doesn't publish school-level results, so the "market" logic behind school choice — that transparency lets families reward effective schools — still doesn't function for parents.
quotes: Most states with private school choice programs don't require students to take any tests, let alone the same ones required by public school students.
low-income students went from 30% of all ESA recipients in year one to just 11% in year two.
In Iowa, ESA students outperform their public school peers on the state ISASP test. In math, 79% of ESA students scored proficient or better, compared to 70% for all students statewide.

Across all ESA participants, the median math growth score was 49. That means Iowa's ESA participants made about the same academic progress as all other Iowa students who started with similar prior test scores.
There's little evidence here of either a dramatic private-school advantage or an academic collapse.
Iowa doesn't publish school-level results for ESA participants, so good luck to any parent trying to figure out which private schools are actually delivering strong results.

This is a real blind spot for schools-as-markets reformers. The theory behind school choice is that families can use information about quality to make better choices, rewarding effective schools and putting pressure on weaker ones.
